name: LGD-4033

lead: LGD-4033 (ligandrol) is a nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator investigated for muscle wasting. A phase I study found increased lean mass in healthy men, but development stalled.
It is widely sold as a research chemical. Small trials show lean mass gains, and observations of recreational use report hormone and lipid problems.

paras: It selectively activates the androgen receptor in muscle and bone and suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, lowering natural testosterone.

Not approved and banned in sport. Documented problems include testosterone suppression, reduced HDL cholesterol and drug-induced liver injury, especially at doses above trial levels. Product contents are unreliable.

lead: LGD-4033, also called Ligandrol and by the developmental code VK5211, is an orally taken, nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) originally developed by Ligand Pharmaceuticals. It has been studied for muscle atrophy, including after hip fracture, and was also explored for cachexia, hypogonadism and osteoporosis; it is not approved for any medical use.[1]

In a randomised phase I trial in 76 healthy men, 21 days of LGD-4033 was well tolerated and raised lean body mass, and a later phase 2 trial in people recovering from hip fracture reported dose-dependent increases in lean mass.[2][1] The compound has far fewer published human studies than the SARM enobosarm, with only four small clinical studies reported as of 2023 according to Wikipedia.[1]

LGD-4033 is also sold online as a research chemical and discussed on bodybuilding forums. Published concerns include dose-dependent drops in testosterone and HDL cholesterol in trials, multiple case reports of drug-induced liver injury in non-medical users, and a JAMA analysis of products sold online as SARMs that examined their composition and labelling.[1][3][4][5] The compound is on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list.[6]
infobox: Ligand Pharmaceuticals; licensed to Viking Therapeutics in 2014[1]
Investigational (US); not approved; prohibited in sport

paras: LGD-4033 is not approved for any medical use. Wikipedia reports that as of 2023 it was in phase 2 development by Viking Therapeutics for muscle atrophy in people with hip fracture, while development for cachexia, hypogonadism and osteoporosis was discontinued.[1]

The compound is sold by online vendors for physique and performance purposes, and Wikipedia states it is often used at doses far above those tested in clinical trials, with unknown effectiveness and safety; it also notes that social media has played an important role in spreading non-medical SARM use.[1] On T Nation, users describe taking it in cycles for periods of weeks, sometimes alongside the growth-hormone secretagogue MK-677, as a substitute or adjunct in relation to anabolic steroids, or after prohormone use.[7][8][9] Others discuss using SARMs during post-cycle recovery.[10]

In the 21-day phase I trial, 1 mg per day increased lean body mass by about 1.2 kg compared with baseline, according to Wikipedia, which compares this with a 1.3 kg gain seen with enobosarm in 12 weeks in older adults.[1] The 2013 report in The Journals of Gerontology described dose-proportional pharmacokinetics, a long half-life, and no drug-related serious adverse events.[2]

In the 12-week phase 2 trial in 108 men and women after hip fracture surgery, Wikipedia reports placebo-adjusted lean body mass gains of 4.8 percent at 0.5 mg per day, 7.2 percent at 1 mg per day and 9.1 percent at 2 mg per day, with dose-dependent muscle strength improvements and reported tolerability.[1]

A 2025 systematic review of randomised trials of SARMs on physical performance pooled nine studies of six SARMs, including LGD-4033, with 970 patients and a mean follow-up of 80 days.[11] A 2013 review of SARMs for cancer-related muscle wasting described enobosarm as the most clinically characterised SARM and reviewed LGD-4033 data alongside it.[12]

Human trials are few. The multi-dose phase I study enrolled 76 healthy men aged 21 to 50 randomised to placebo or 0.1, 0.3 or 1.0 mg daily for 21 days; it measured lean and fat mass, strength, stair-climbing power, hormones, lipids, PSA and liver enzymes. Hemoglobin, PSA, AST, ALT and QT intervals did not change significantly, and the drug was well tolerated.[2] Hormonal and lipid effects reported by Wikipedia from the clinical program include dose-dependent decreases in total and free testosterone, FSH, SHBG, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides, with LH, total cholesterol, LDL and PSA unchanged.[1]

A phase 2 trial begun in November 2016 enrolled 108 people recovering from hip fracture surgery, as described above.[1] A published case report on a man using LGD-4033 together with MK-677 examined body composition, circulating biomarkers and muscle androgen hormone and receptor content.[13]
Wikipedia lists three small phase I trials and one phase 2 trial as the total of reported clinical studies.[1] No clinical trial has tested LGD-4033 at the higher doses used by non-medical users.

Reported effects in trials include headache and dry mouth, lowered HDL cholesterol and testosterone, and lowered SHBG.[1] Because HDL falls relative to LDL, Wikipedia says LGD-4033 could theoretically raise the risk of heart attack and stroke; the US FDA states that liver toxicity, adverse blood lipid effects and potential cardiovascular risk are among the potential harms of SARMs.[1] Liver enzyme elevations were not reported in the small trials, but several case reports of drug-induced liver injury in non-medical users have been published, including a 32-year-old man with cholestatic hepatitis confirmed on biopsy, a 2023 German report, and a 2024 case report.[1][14][15][4] A review of two cases of SARM- and post-cycle-therapy-related liver injury discusses the broader literature.[16]

Masculinising effects in women are largely uncharacterised, and Wikipedia notes anecdotal reports of masculinisation with black-market SARMs in online forums.[1] A T Nation poster described a long hormonal slump after cycling SARMs including LGD-4033, and another said he felt unwell by the fourth week and wondered whether the product was actually a prohormone.[17][9]

LGD-4033 binds the androgen receptor with high affinity (Ki about 0.9 nM) and little affinity for progesterone, glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid receptors.[1] In castrated rats it increased levator ani muscle weight to around 140 percent of intact controls, while prostate weight reached about 45 percent, a pattern researchers describe as tissue selectivity.[1] Androgen receptor activation also feeds back on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which is the proposed explanation for falling testosterone levels.[2][3]

Pharmacokinetics were linear across 0.1 to 1 mg daily, with about threefold accumulation over 21 days and an elimination half-life of 24 to 36 hours.[1][2] Human metabolism and excretion studies, done mainly for doping control, have identified multiple metabolites in urine.[18][19]

LGD-4033 is a nonsteroidal pyrrolidinyl-benzonitrile SARM (molecular weight about 338 g/mol), sometimes called a quinoline-type SARM because of its predecessor LG121071. Its structure had not been disclosed as late as 2013, and it is distinct from the other Ligand compounds LGD-2226, LGD-2941 and LGD-3303.[1]

Ligand Pharmaceuticals discovered LG121071, the first orally active nonsteroidal androgen receptor agonist, described in 1999; LGD-4033 followed and was first described in the literature in 2010, with phase I trials beginning in 2009.[1] A multi-dose phase I report appeared in 2013, and a phase 2 trial in muscle wasting began in November 2016 with results reported in 2017 and 2018.[1][2] Viking Therapeutics licensed the compound from Ligand on 22 May 2014.[1]

In the United States LGD-4033 is an investigational new drug. In October 2017 the FDA warned a Missouri supplement company that distributing LGD-4033 products violated the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, because they were marketed as dietary supplements though they would be new drugs.[1] SARMs were added to the WADA Prohibited List in 2008, and LGD-4033 has been reported in athlete urine samples and supplements; Wikipedia lists several athletes with positive tests, some of whom deny knowingly taking it.[1][6][20]

Wikipedia states that many products sold online as LGD-4033 contain none of it or contain unrelated substances, and doses are often not as labelled.[1] A 2017 JAMA study and a German study of black-market products from 2010 to 2013 examined the identity of such products.[5][21]

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: Forum discussion on T Nation includes a user who ordered about eleven SARMs to run together, a poster who described LGD-4033 as a very suppressive SARM, a user who reported an 8-week run followed by blood work, and a poster who said low doses appeared to harm HDL/LDL ratios.[22][17][8][23] Other posts treat it as the SARM equivalent of a particular oral steroid, or cite the 2013 phase I paper in an argument about safety.[24][25]

lore.intro: On forums LGD-4033 is treated as one of the stronger and more suppressive SARMs, used in cycles and often combined with other compounds.[17][22]

claims.claim: LGD-4033 is a safer, non-suppressive way to gain lean mass compared with steroids
LGD-4033 produces large lean mass gains in a few weeks
LGD-4033 damages cholesterol even at low doses
Products sold as Ligandrol are often not what they claim to be
SARMs can be safely added to a steroid cycle or used for post-cycle recovery
Running many SARMs together at high doses is acceptable
